blocks.text: A finished map concealed a long production line. Surveyors and field assistants observed boundaries and control; human computers reduced measurements; draughtspeople compiled the sheet; lithographic and photographic staff reproduced it; clerks indexed plans and prints. The Department of Lands and Survey relied on these skills in district and head offices alike.

blocks.text: The print run was substantial. In 1884–85, the Survey Department reported 603,341 lithographic impressions. That figure shows the scale of its map production, while the report’s separate sheet, record-map and plan counts show how many distinct records staff had to maintain.

blocks.text: Rachel Gillanders appears in government records first as a Computer and later as a Draughtswoman and Computer. Madge Pirrit’s initials appear on maps of Papakura and Wharekawa; a 1926 Gazette transfer entry gives the name behind those credits. Their work joined calculation, drawing and map production long before digital editing tools.

blocks.text: Mary Sutherland carried out technical calculations and laboratory work as a qualified forester while accommodation rules restricted her field deployment. Mary Mulcahy selected ballot cards and processed military-service records. M. Dovey and M. Freeman appear in soil-survey records among the draughting staff turning field and laboratory classifications into maps. These records name work that a finished sheet does not show.
